files.lab/one-tap-capture.md:
---
number: 5
name: One-tap capture
hypothesis: >
  If saving an idea takes one tap and zero decisions, capture volume goes
  up and triage stays manageable.
status: concluded
result: Half-confirmed.
project: kubli
date: 2025-11-19
---

## Experiment

A bare prototype: one giant button, voice or text, no categories, no
titles. Everything sorted later by time and place.

## Result

Half-confirmed. Capture volume tripled. Triage stayed manageable — but
only because place-grouping made review feel like revisiting rather than
sorting. Without the location index, the pile would have been a landfill.

## Notes

This experiment is why Kubli exists.
files.lab/paper-sensor-diary.md:
---
number: 6
name: Paper sensor diary
hypothesis: >
  Logging one sensor reading a day by hand, on paper, will change what I
  choose to sense — and what I build to sense it.
status: concluded
result: Confirmed, unexpectedly.
project: prism
date: 2026-02-11
---

## Experiment

Thirty days. One reading per day — temperature, noise, light, whatever —
written in a pocket notebook. No automation allowed.

## Result

Confirmed, unexpectedly. Hand-logging made me pick readings that meant
something ("kitchen at 7am, before anyone's up") instead of readings that
were easy. PRISM's reflection views inherit this directly: the views are
organized around moments, not sensors.

## Notes

Automation is a decision about what's worth noticing, made once, in a
hurry, forever. Paper renegotiates it daily.
files.lab/whispering-city.md:
---
number: 7
name: The Whispering City
hypothesis: >
  A piece of interactive fiction can feel alive if the city itself, not the
  characters, is the thing that remembers your choices.
status: running
project: the-whispering-city
date: 2026-05-02
---

## Experiment

A small text engine where every location accumulates a memory of what
players have done there, and leaks fragments of it back to later visitors
as environmental whispers.

## Result

Still running. The memory model works; the hard part is making the
whispers feel uncanny instead of random. Current approach: whispers only
surface details the *current* player could plausibly almost-know.

## Notes

The engine wants to become a library. Resisting until the fiction is good.
files.notes/on-place-based-capture.md:
---
title: Place is a filing system nobody maintains
date: 2026-07-28
kind: design
project: kubli
---

Every organizational scheme I've built for notes has eventually collapsed
under its own maintenance cost. Tags rot. Folders multiply. Inboxes become
landfills.

Location is different. You never have to file anything by place — you were
already somewhere when the idea arrived. The metadata writes itself, and it
matches how memory actually indexes: *I thought of that on the walk by the
reservoir.*

Kubli's whole bet is that this free, self-maintaining index is enough
structure for a capture tool. So far the bet is holding.
files.notes/quiet-is-a-status.md:
---
title: Quiet is a status, not a failure
date: 2026-06-14
kind: observation
project: habi
---

habi has been quiet for a while, and I kept feeling like I owed it an
apology — or worse, a fake progress update.

Then I added "Quiet" as a first-class project status on this site, right
next to "Building" and "Shipped." The moment it had a name, the guilt
evaporated. A workshop is full of resting projects. That's what the
shelves are for.
files.notes/webhooks-not-polling.md:
---
title: Let GitHub call you
date: 2026-08-05
kind: devlog
---

This site shows near-realtime progress on my projects, and the tempting
first implementation was to poll GitHub from the browser. Don't.

The shape that works: GitHub webhooks land on one endpoint, get their
signatures verified, get normalized into boring internal events, and update
a per-project snapshot in Postgres. Pages read the snapshot. The browser
talks only to this site, never to GitHub.

Polling survives only as a reconciliation pass for the events webhooks
inevitably drop — a safety net, not a strategy.
files.porscha.md:
---
title: Porscha
---

## Hello

I'm Porscha. I make things — mostly software, sometimes art, occasionally
things that are hard to file under either.

This site is my workshop. It's where finished work sits next to half-built
experiments, because that's how a real workbench looks.

## I build things

Right now that means small, personal tools: a capture app that remembers
*where* you were when an idea hit, a way of looking at your own data that
doesn't feel like a quarterly report, a habit companion that forgives you.

I like software that feels like it was made by a person, for a person.

## How I got here

I started by taking things apart — radios, websites, other people's code —
and eventually noticed I enjoyed the putting-back-together more. A few
false starts taught me that shipping something small and honest beats
polishing something imaginary. cloakli, my first real app, never found its
feet. Everything since is built on what it taught me.

## Things I care about

- Tools that respect attention instead of farming it.
- Work-in-progress shown honestly, not staged.
- Software that stays understandable a year later.
- Making things by hand, even when a generator would be faster.

## Selected history

- **Now** — building Kubli, tending PRISM, letting habi rest.
- **Before** — cloakli, a private capture tool; retired but formative.
- **Earlier** — years of experiments, some of which live in the Lab.

## Elsewhere

The code lives on GitHub. Everything else worth seeing is already here.
files.projects/habi.md:
---
project: habi
why: >
  Every habit app is built for the streak. habi is built for the return —
  because missing days is not failure, it's the normal texture of a life.
lessons:
  - Guilt is a terrible retention strategy.
  - The smallest possible check-in is the right size.
screenshots: []
---

habi is a small, forgiving habit companion. It assumes you will miss days
and designs for the moment you come back, instead of punishing you for
having left.

It's resting at the moment — intentionally. The core loop works, and the
next round of work is waiting for Kubli's capture flow to ship first.
files.projects/kubli.md:
---
project: kubli
why: >
  Ideas arrive in places — on a walk, in a hardware store aisle, halfway up
  a stairwell. Kubli exists because notes apps flatten all of that into one
  undifferentiated inbox, and place is exactly the handle memory wants.
lessons:
  - Capture has to be faster than forgetting. Anything over two taps loses.
  - Location is a filing system nobody has to maintain.
  - An offline queue is not an edge case; it is the primary case.
screenshots: []
---

Kubli is a place-based capture tool. You stash an idea, a link, a photo, a
fragment — and Kubli quietly remembers where you were. Later, the pile
re-sorts itself around the places of your life, which turns out to be how
you actually remember things.

The current work is entirely about the capture flow: making the moment of
having an idea and the moment of saving it feel like the same moment.

It grew out of cloakli, an earlier private-capture experiment that never
quite worked. Kubli keeps its lesson — capture is sacred, everything else
is optional — and discards the rest.
files.projects/prism.md:
---
project: prism
why: >
  Personal data mostly gets collected, rarely gets looked at. PRISM exists
  to make the looking worthwhile — views you'd open on a Sunday morning out
  of curiosity, not obligation.
lessons:
  - A chart you don't want to look at is just surveillance with extra steps.
  - Time is the only axis everyone already understands.
  - Export early. Data you can't take with you isn't yours.
screenshots: []
---

PRISM takes the scattered records a life produces and turns them into
something you can actually sit with — timelines, densities, quiet
patterns. Less dashboard, more reflection.

The current milestone is the first set of views that earn their place: a
timeline that reads like a diary you didn't have to write, and a density
view that shows the shape of a season at a glance.
